client: I've been really dreading this networking event that's coming up next week for work. Every time I think about walking into a room full of strangers and having to introduce myself and talk about what I do, my heart just starts racing and I feel kind of sick. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the event is still going to happen whether I feel ready or not.
therapist: What you're describing — that racing heart, the dread, the sense that nothing can really help — tells me this feels genuinely overwhelming right now, and I can hear that tension in how you're speaking too. That thought, *"talking won't change anything,"* is actually a really important one to gently examine, because while it's true the event will happen, what *can* shift is how your mind is framing it and what your body does with that fear. Would you be open to exploring what specific thoughts are driving that dread, so we can start loosening their grip before next week?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I guess I'm open to it, though I'm a little skeptical that just talking through my thoughts is going to make me feel less terrified in the moment. The main thing that keeps running through my head is that everyone there is going to be more successful, more polished, more confident than me, and they're going to see right through me and think I have no business being there. It's like I already know how it's going to go, and that certainty is what makes it feel so hopeless.
therapist: That sense of certainty — *"I already know how it's going to go"* — is actually a really telling thought to catch, because your voice carries a kind of quiet resignation that suggests this feels less like a fear and more like a fact to you right now. But that feeling of certainty is itself a cognitive distortion called **fortune-telling**, where our anxious mind presents a worst-case prediction as guaranteed truth. What evidence do you actually have that everyone will see through you — and is there any evidence from past experiences that might tell a different story?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean, I can think of a few times where networking situations didn't completely blow up in my face, but I always chalked that up to luck or the other person being polite. It's hard to take those as real evidence because in my head, next week feels different, higher stakes, more people who actually matter in my field. So even when I try to think of counterexamples, my brain just kind of dismisses them and goes right back to the worst case.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly, almost carefully — along with what you're saying suggests a kind of exhausted resignation, like part of you wants to believe those counterexamples but feels too worn down to fight your brain's dismissal of them. What you're describing is a really common pattern called **discounting the positive**, where your mind applies a different standard to good evidence than bad — past successes need an explanation like luck, but predicted failures are just accepted as truth. It's worth asking: if a close friend told you their past networking wins were "just luck," what would you say to challenge that?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I'd probably tell a friend that luck doesn't fully explain it, that they must have said something right or made a real connection somehow. But when it comes to myself, that logic just doesn't feel the same, it's like there's a different set of rules for me and I can't seem to override it no matter how much I intellectually understand what you're saying. It's frustrating because I can see the pattern you're describing, I just don't know how to actually feel it differently in the moment.
therapist: That gap you're describing — knowing something intellectually but not being able to *feel* it — is one of the most frustrating parts of anxiety, and I can hear that frustration in your voice even as you're speaking quite softly and quickly, like your mind is working hard to process all of this. The good news is that CBT isn't just about thinking your way to a different conclusion — it's also about *behaving* your way there, because sometimes the feeling catches up only after we've collected enough real, lived experience that our brain can no longer dismiss. So rather than trying to feel differently before the event, what if we focused on one small, concrete thing you could do *at* the event that might generate that kind of undeniable evidence?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think I can see what you're getting at, but my worry is that even if I manage to do something small, like introduce myself to one person, my brain is just going to find a way to explain it away again, the same way it does with past successes. I guess if I had to pick something concrete it would be that, just one real conversation instead of hovering near the food table the whole time, but I'm already imagining how awkward that first approach is going to feel. What if the person I pick seems disinterested or gives me short answers, because then it's just going to feel like confirmation of everything I already fear?
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now tells me your mind is already racing ahead to that moment of potential rejection, almost like you're pre-living it — and I want to gently point out that you've just done something really significant by naming a concrete goal, even while anxious. But let's also look at that "confirmation" fear directly: if someone gives short answers, is that *only* explainable by you having no business being there, or could it mean they're distracted, introverted, having a bad day, or just not your person — the same way you'd interpret it charitably for a friend? The goal isn't a perfect conversation; it's collecting evidence that you can *initiate*, which is something your brain can't as easily explain away.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That reframe about the other person maybe just having a bad day or being introverted actually does make some sense to me, and I hadn't really thought about it that way before. But I think my real fear isn't even that one conversation goes badly, it's more that I'll freeze up before I even get to the approach, like my body will just refuse to cooperate and I'll spend the whole night pretending to check my phone. I guess the question for me is, how do I actually get myself to take that first step when everything in me is screaming to stay invisible?
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, high, like the words are tumbling out — tells me that freeze response feels very real and immediate to you, almost like your body is already rehearsing it. What you're describing is your nervous system trying to protect you, and the trick isn't to overpower it with willpower but to give it a tiny, specific script that reduces the decision in the moment — something as simple as making eye contact and saying "how do you know the organizers?" takes the pressure off you to be impressive and just gets you *moving*. Would it help to actually practice that opening line right now, so that when the freeze hits, your body already has a groove worn into it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Practicing it out loud right now actually feels kind of embarrassing, even just with you, which is probably telling in itself. I can see why having a script might help, because at least it takes away the part where I'm standing there trying to think of something to say while my mind goes completely blank. But I'm a little worried that if I rehearse something specific, it's going to come out sounding robotic or memorized in the moment, and then that'll just be a whole different thing to feel self-conscious about.
therapist: The fact that even practicing here feels embarrassing is actually really valuable information — it tells us the self-consciousness kicks in well before the event itself, and your voice right now, quiet and careful, suggests you're being quite vulnerable in admitting that. On the "robotic" worry: a script isn't meant to be a performance, it's more like a launchpad — once the other person responds, the conversation takes on its own natural shape and you're no longer reciting anything. And honestly, the slight awkwardness of a rehearsed opener is almost always invisible to the other person; what they notice is that you showed up and started a conversation, which is the part that matters.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I think what you're saying about it being a launchpad rather than a script makes it feel a little less pressure-filled, like I'm not committing to a whole performance, just getting myself through the door of the conversation. But I still have this nagging worry that even if I manage to do it once, it's going to feel so exhausting and draining that I'll just retreat after that one interaction and consider the whole night a failure. I guess I'm wondering if one conversation is really enough to count as a win, or if I'm just setting the bar low to give myself an excuse to hide.
therapist: That question — "am I just setting the bar low to hide?" — is a sharp and honest one, and the fact that you're asking it tells me you're genuinely trying to hold yourself accountable rather than let anxiety off the hook. But there's an important difference between a low bar and a *strategic* one: one real conversation isn't settling, it's a deliberate experiment that generates real evidence, and you can always choose to have a second one if energy allows. The goal for next week isn't to conquer the whole room — it's to prove to your nervous system that you can walk through that door, which is the foundation everything else gets built on.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Framing it as an experiment actually helps a little, because experiments aren't supposed to be perfect, they're just supposed to give you information. But I think what I'm still sitting with is this fear that even if I do everything right, have the one conversation, use the launchpad line, don't hide by the food table, I'll still come home feeling lonely and like I didn't really connect with anyone in any meaningful way. That's almost the scarier outcome for me, doing everything I'm supposed to do and still feeling like I don't belong there.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, almost breathless, with a kind of urgency — tells me this fear of doing everything right and *still* feeling like you don't belong might actually be the deepest fear underneath all the others, and it deserves to be named as such. What you're describing isn't really about networking technique anymore — it's a fear of fundamental disconnection, that there's something about you that makes real belonging impossible, which is a painful and very old belief worth exploring. But I'd gently ask: is one evening, one experiment, really enough evidence to confirm or deny something that big — or might you be asking a single networking event to answer a question it was never equipped to answer?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That actually stopped me in my tracks a little, because I think you're right that I've been putting a lot of weight on this one event, like it's going to tell me something definitive about whether I'm someone who belongs or someone who doesn't. And yeah, that fear does feel old, like it's been around a lot longer than this networking event. But I'm not sure what to do with that, because even if I understand that one night can't answer that question, I'm still going to walk in there carrying it.
therapist: The softness in your voice right now, even as the words come quickly, feels like someone who has just touched something tender and real — and I want to acknowledge how significant it is that you named this as an *old* fear, because that tells us it didn't start with networking and it won't be resolved by one event. You're right that you'll walk in carrying it, but there's a difference between carrying something that defines you and carrying something you're learning to recognize and question — and just in this conversation, you've already started doing the latter. That older fear of not belonging is something worth exploring more deeply over time, and you don't have to resolve it before next week.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech
